catalog_quote: [p. 76, 2.6 Tone] Most African languages are tonal. Kiong is, therefore, not an exception. A language is said to be tonal when differences in relative pitch are utilised for lexical and grammatical functions. Both level and contour tones occur in the language. Instances of lexical tonal distinctions in Kiong include: 14. (i) H-H /úsá/ 'right hand' (ii) H-L /úsà/ 'food' Examples of falling (HL) tones are: 15. (i) / mâ / 'here' (ii) / wê / 'sweep' Rising tones occur in words such as: 16. (i) [boŋĭnwa] 'lips' (ii) [dĭéni ] 'tomorrow' ... [p. 79, 4.3 i. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kiong is described as a lexical/grammatical tone language (High, Low, Rising, Falling, plus downstepped High), every syllable bearing tone; the source's phonology sketch (vowels, length, syllable types, tone, consonants) makes no mention of word stress or accent at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None; authors note their tonal analysis is incomplete and recommend writing Kiong without tone marks in practical orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical citation forms elicited with a modified Swadesh-100 list from the last elderly speakers (Okoyong and Calabar); word-level tone only, no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Okon & Noah's data are from the last elderly Kiong speakers of Odukpani/Akamkpa LGAs (Okoyong), i.e. kion1242 proper. Decker et al. 2022 (SIL survey) and, per them, Blench 2021 conclude that Kiong [kkm, kion1242] and Durop/Korop [krp, koro1304] are one language (Odukpani speakers call it Kiong, Akamkpa speakers Durop); Kiong itself is practically dormant (2-3 rememberers in 2021). Descriptions of Durop (Kastelein 1994; Connell 2021,../koro1304/) are therefore near-substitutes but belong to glottocode koro1304.
